description: Question: the spectrum of Germany's electricity demand has a line at 6/7 and at 8/7 cycles per day, periods of 28 and 21 hours. Nothing in society runs on a 21-hour cycle, so where do they come from? Data: 8 whole weeks (Monday 24 August to Sunday 18 October 2026, all in summer time) of Germany's quarter-hourly load from Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE, ENTSO-E data, CC BY 4.0), as hourly means. Idea: the modulation (convolution) theorem. The load is close to a daily waveform multiplied by a weekly envelope (weekdays high, Saturday lower, Sunday lowest). A product in time is a convolution in frequency, so every daily harmonic k (1, 2, 3, 4 per day) carries a copy of the weekly spectrum around it: sidebands at k ± j/7, exactly as an AM radio carrier carries its audio. And resolution and windowing: a record of length T smears every line into a sinc about 1/T wide, so lines 1/7 per day apart need well over a week of data; a Hann window lowers the floor between the lines at the cost of wider lines. Steps: rows to hourly load (Polars); three variants (8 weeks rectangular, 8 weeks Hann, the first week alone, SQL); a discrete Fourier transform on a half-bin grid (SQL); the theory lines k ± j/7; the strongest peaks matched to them; the share of power between lines; whether each record resolves the 6/7 sideband from the daily line; the daily envelope. The aha: beside the daily line (7.0 GW amplitude) sit lines at 6/7 per day (1.29 GW, a 28-hour period) and 8/7 (0.60 GW, 21 hours), and the same pattern around 2 per day: not cycles anyone keeps, but the weekend (weekday mean 53.8 GW and daily swing 19.7 GW, Sunday 43.6 and 13.7 GW) seen in the frequency domain. A single week of data cannot show them: its resolution is 1/7 per day, and the sideband and the daily line melt into one hump. Caveats: holidays (none nationwide in this window; 3 October, German Unity Day, a Saturday in 2026) and weather add a slow drift that leaks near 0; the hourly mean is itself a low-pass filter (no aliasing up to 12 per day); amplitude is in GW of the centred load. Next: compare a winter window (lighting peaks change the daily waveform: stronger harmonics), another country (country=fr), or the solar output's spectrum (no weekly modulation, so no sidebands).
name: Sidebands in the power demand: the modulation theorem
